In the letter, executive chair and CEO Karl Meyers said the company had made the “very difficult decision” to curtail Quesnel River Pulp mill for an indefinite period. “Based on current contractual obligations, we will continue operating the effluent system for twelve months, or until we can reach an acceptable alternative,” Meyers said in the letter. “We will continue to complete an orderly shutdown of the balance of the operations over the next several weeks, setting it up for a potential restart in the future.” In August, Millar Western announced temporary curtailment of operations until at least November. Meyers said Millar Western will also look at filling vacancies at other company operations with displaced employees. “For those who will continue to work, the period between now and your final day of employment will be considered as working notice,” he said. According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] Tests find coca and alcohol in Inca child mummies, but none of the hallucinogens screened for
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers analyzing hair and nails from eight Inca children sacrificed about 500 years ago found traces of coca in hair and evidence of alcohol in some children, but none of the hallucinogens they tested for. The remains came from mountain sites in Peru and Argentina and belonged to children aged 6 to 14. The findings suggest the substances may have helped prepare children for the physical and emotional strain of journeys to sacrificial sites rather than induce hallucinations, said archaeologist Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw. Harmine, a plant compound associated with Amazonian species, was found in a nail from Juanita, a 14-year-old mummy. The team plans further study of the substances and sacred mountain sites.

items.title: [astronomy.com] Mars orbiter finds volcanic gas near Alba Mons, hinting magma persists
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers report that the European-Russian Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrogen chloride gas near Alba Mons on Mars during the planet’s cold aphelion season, when the gas is usually absent. The localized, out-of-season signal may come from magma releasing gas through fractures, suggesting that parts of Mars could remain volcanically active. The finding does not establish that an eruption is occurring. The team used observations from the orbiter’s Atmospheric Chemistry Suite and examined images of the region for possible pathways from underground. The study, published in Science Advances on Nov. 4, reports newly identified narrow fissures that could connect the gas to magmatic sources. Researchers say further observations, including attempts to detect sulfur dioxide from Earth, could help test the volcanic explanation.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [newspaceeconomy.ca] Researchers test AI systems for satellite servicing, imaging and astronomy
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Three research efforts are testing autonomous decision-making for space operations, from analyzing Earth imagery in orbit to guiding satellite rescues and scheduling astronomical observations. Planet Labs’ Pelican-4 satellite used an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin processor to detect aircraft in imagery in March. Google Research and Planet Labs said a prototype later ran the Gemma 4 model on an orbital tensor-processing unit. A team led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is developing CORTEX, software to plan and guide a servicing spacecraft’s approach to an unresponsive satellite. A separate astronomical-survey challenge evaluated systems submitted by 102 teams in simulated observing campaigns. Researchers found that leading entries combined numerical exposure planning with language models, while changes to science priorities substantially changed the systems’ rankings.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN warns 2026 heat records signal accelerating climate extremes
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.title: [carbonbrief.org] El Niño-linked fires lift total carbon emissions despite fossil fuel dip
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Climate change is altering natural colors across Arctic landscapes, lakes and coral reefs, with shifts linked to warming, permafrost thaw and pollution. Another study found that green-wavelength values in more than 400,000 North American boreal-Arctic lakes fell 15% between 1984 and 2019, indicating darker water. items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

It is Paraguay’s largest private investment but local people accuse a forestry giant of ignoring their contamination concerns over its vast plantation

When Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

Although rain had ended in parts of the Southwest by Monday, flooding along some swollen waterways could continue through at least Tuesday.

Bird flu spread quickly through Central Washington dairy farms in October, with 40 Washington herds testing positive from Oct. 7 to Oct. 30, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture; 33 were in Yakima County and one was in neighboring Benton County. Officials confirmed the first two cases at Yakima County dairies on Oct. 8 and four additional cases on Oct. 29. A Yakima County resident exposed to infected dairy cattle died Nov. 1, and local officials also reported two other human infections linked to cattle. Containing the virus is difficult because cattle farms cannot be sealed and controlled as tightly as poultry barns, said Rick Naerbout, executive director of the Washington State Dairy Federation. The federation advised farmers on Oct. 4 to follow biosecurity plans and alert veterinarians to falling milk production; researchers have not established the virus’s natural route of spread among cows. Washington officials say infected cows generally recover within four to six weeks, and state agriculture officials say pasteurized milk remains safe.

Environment Canada escalated rainfall warnings for southwest British Columbia as a new storm system was forecast to bring more than 250 millimetres of rain to parts of Vancouver Island. Heavy rain was expected Tuesday and Wednesday, with rain continuing later in the week. Orange warnings cover west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky; the provincial River Forecast Centre issued a flood watch for much of southwest B.C. The incoming storm follows weekend winds and rain that killed a driver in Surrey. Police also linked the storm to the death of a 78-year-old Vancouver pedestrian, and a canoeist is missing off northern Vancouver Island. Nearly 415,000 BC Hydro customers lost power at some point, and about 13,300 remained without electricity by late Monday afternoon. In Zeballos, evacuation orders and alerts remained in force for properties threatened by landslides. Officials expected to issue another update Friday, Nov. 13.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.title: [cisa.gov] U.S. agencies warn hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Five U.S. agencies warned on Nov. 5 that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, including controllers used by grocery stores, hospitals, food producers and transport operators. Attackers may exploit unpatched or internet-accessible devices to change temperatures or defrost settings, or prevent operators from seeing temperature readings. Such attacks could spoil stock, compromise storage safety and damage equipment. The warning follows attacks on European supermarkets on Nov. 2 and an incident that altered refrigeration settings at three French blood-service facilities. The U.S. agencies did not say whether refrigeration systems in the United States had been targeted. They urged operators to remove unnecessary internet access, secure remote connections, update firmware, isolate control systems from business networks and set alerts for unsafe temperature changes.
